content:
Banyan trees outside Tai Po Mega Mall, one of the old banyans was uprooted and fell.

Typhoon "Cempaka" made landfall in the east, with parts of the eastern New Territories recording over 140mm of rainfall yesterday. The government said that as of 1pm on Sunday (the 26th), the government's 1823 call centre and the Fire Services Department had together received 331 reports of fallen trees. Tai Po was one of the hardest-hit areas for tree collapses.

Of the ten banyan trees next to Wan Lam House of Wan Tau Tong Estate, eight were toppled by strong winds. When reporters went to the scene this morning (the 27th), the remains of the eight trees had already been cleared. A Wan Tau Tong resident who has lived there for over 30 years said, "They've been here for so many years, nothing this severe has ever happened." The resident noted that typhoons over the years had never toppled these banyan trees, yet they still could not withstand the force of "Cempaka". "This time they were uprooted," they said.

The resident said, "The worst was this time — you wouldn't believe it even seeing it." The "banyan grove" originally formed by ten banyan trees was destroyed overnight, leaving only two. Residents felt it was a pity that these ten long-standing banyan trees, which had sheltered Wan Tau Tong Estate residents from wind and rain for years, had toppled: "Let's see if they'll replant them."

A large banyan outside Tai Po Mega Mall similarly could not withstand the force of Typhoon "Cempaka". The banyan and silk-cotton trees here are collective memories for local residents. One of the large banyans toppled this time; the tree stood roughly 12 metres tall, planted in a square plot about 2 metres by 2 metres — the kind of planting situation typical of "flowerpot trees" that fall during storms.

A resident of Fu Shin Estate said they had heard beforehand that "Cempaka" would not be very powerful, and only just learned that the large banyan outside the mall had been blown down by Typhoon "Cempaka", so "it gave me a shock seeing it." Sharing, "I pass by here every day going to work," they had always known of this large banyan's existence, and expressed lament that Typhoon "Cempaka" had toppled this long-standing tree: "What a waste of a tree." Another Tai Po resident, when asked whether she hoped the fallen banyan could be saved, said, "Of course." She believed that planting banyans was better than other species, as they grew more slowly. When a reporter inspected the scene in the afternoon, workers had already removed the tree.

The banyan toppled, exposing roots that had been buried in the soil. Leaves and earth were scattered all over the ground in a scene of utter devastation. Most passers-by stopped to take photos, joining in seeing off the "final journey" of this large banyan that had carried the memories of Tai Po residents for many years.

Separately, a horsetail tree along the cycle track beside Lam Tsuen River outside the mall also collapsed, completely blocking the cycle track, with several bicycles abandoned in front of the fallen tree.

In addition, a large banyan next to the Kwong Fuk Estate community hall also could not withstand the force of "Cempaka" and toppled. This morning, workers were on site using chainsaws to clear the tree's remains; passing children expressed surprise, saying "What is he doing?", stunned by the power of Typhoon "Cempaka".

At the entrance to Cheung Chi House of Cheung Tung Estate in Fanling, two trees — a large banyan and a silk-cotton — were toppled by the typhoon. Near a roundabout close to Cheung Chi House, the trunk of a large banyan had snapped, and the upper portion of the tree had collapsed, obstructing traffic at the roundabout. No workers were present to remove the trees in the morning.

"Tree doctor" Chim Chi-yung takes the pulse

Professor Chim Chi-yung, professor and consultant in the Department of Geography and Environmental Science at the Education University of Hong Kong, said the reason these trees were blown down was "all the same" — namely that planting space and soil were insufficient, roots were confined, leaving the trees unable to withstand strong winds and resulting in collapse. He noted that such "flowerpot tree" problems were "extremely common". Professor Chim suggested two solutions: either dig out the original soil and re-lay it, or plant only short, slender trees — but that would waste land resources. He expressed that it was "such a pity" Hong Kong had not fully utilised planting resources, and described the current way of planting trees as "a waste of resources".

Propose government establish a "tree rescue squad"

When Super Typhoon Ragasa hit Hong Kong last September, the government stepped in to save an Indian rubber tree at Oi Man Estate in Ho Man Tin that had grown alongside residents for half a century, as well as a heritage tree, a large-leaved silk tree, at Kowloon Park in Tsim Sha Tsui. Can the trees toppled by Cempaka this time be saved? Professor Chim said, "There's a way to prop them back up," using machinery to help raise the tree upright and support it to keep it alive. "They can be saved, but it comes down to resources," he said, explaining that one has to consider whether resource allocation is sufficient. Professor Chim noted he had on multiple occasions proposed setting up a "tree rescue squad" to conduct training and preparation in normal times, so as to ensure it could be deployed to "save trees" in emergencies, but as of now there were no signs of such a team being established: "I believe the government has not done this."
